I've gathered substantial material. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I wasn't able to fetch every page (hit search/fetch limits), so I'll note what I found and what's missing.

---

## Judges 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

Judges 4 (prose) and Judges 5 (poetry) form a unique couplet in Scripture — the only chapter pair telling the same event in both narrative and song. Precept Austin notes this is the fourth "cycle" in Judges: apostasy → servitude → supplication → salvation. Warren Wiersbe outlines the chapter as a five-act drama (vv. 1–3 tragic situation; vv. 4–7 divine revelation; vv. 8–10 reluctant participant; vv. 11–23 victorious confrontation; ch. 5 glorious celebration). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

---

### Verse 1: *"After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD."*

- **The cycle resumes.** Enduring Word observes that "when Ehud was dead" the people immediately drifted back to disobedience. This continual pattern makes one "less and less confident of man but more and more impressed with the mercy and grace of God." Trapp is quoted: "The sedentary life is most subject to diseases: standing waters soon putrify." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **"Again" — progressive declension.** Precept Austin notes that the Septuagint renders "again" with *prostithemi* ("to add to"), suggesting they "added to" the evil of prior generations — a progressive worsening. Judges 2:19 describes them "acting more corruptly than their fathers." The eighty years of rest under Ehud produced not revival but complacency. "The prosperity of fools will destroy them." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Reformation vs. revival.** Precept Austin distinguishes the two: "Reformation temporarily changes outward conduct while revival permanently alters inward character." When Ehud was alive the people obeyed under constraint; when he died, their unchanged hearts reasserted themselves. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Gill** notes the chapter shows Israel sinning, being delivered into Jabin's hand, then Deborah and Barak consulting for deliverance. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/4.htm)

---

### Verse 2: *"So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor..."*

- **"The LORD sold them."** Enduring Word says God loved Israel too much to leave them alone. "There may be times when we wish God would leave us alone; yet we are ultimately thankful for His continued dealing with us." The verb "sold" (Hebrew *makar*) is figurative for transferring ownership — coming under another's power. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/) and (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Jabin — likely a hereditary title.** Precept Austin notes that Joshua had already defeated and killed a "Jabin" king of Hazor (Joshua 11:1–13) about 100–150 years earlier. The name probably functioned like "Pharaoh" — a dynastic title. Hazor had been rebuilt because Israel failed to occupy it. The oppression this time came from *internal* enemies (Canaanites they had failed to expel), not a foreign invasion. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Hazor** was a strategic city on the Via Maris trade route, about 8–10 miles north of the Sea of Galilee. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Sisera** lived in Harosheth-hagoyim ("woodland of the Gentiles"), located where the Kishon River enters the Plain of Acre, about 10 miles NW of Megiddo. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Ellicott** titles this section "Fresh apostasy of Israel, and their consequent oppression by Jabin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html)

---

### Verse 3: *"Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron..."*

- **Twenty years of harsh oppression.** Enduring Word observes it took Israel twenty years in bondage before they cried out to the LORD. God can use entirely different oppressors each cycle to get His people's attention. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **900 iron chariots** represented overwhelming technological superiority. Israel fought as foot-soldiers with essentially no weapons to match. GotQuestions notes the Canaanites "had 900 chariots of iron and ruled over Israel for 20 years." (https://www.gotquestions.org/Deborah-and-Barak.html)

- **Precept Austin** cross-references 1 Samuel 12:9, which summarizes: "They forgot the LORD their God, so He sold them into the hand of Sisera." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

---

### Verse 4: *"Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time."*

- **A prophetess.** Enduring Word notes that some find it unexpected that God raised up a woman prophetess, but the NT confirms the gift for women (Acts 21:9; 1 Cor 11:5). The essential element of a woman's prophetic ministry in the early church was her clear submission to male leadership (shown by head coverings in that culture). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- Precept Austin notes the Hebrew reads literally "a woman, a prophetess." Deborah held three leadership positions: judge (only female judge in Scripture), military leader, and prophetess. Her name means "bee" or "wasp" — prompting one scholar to quip she was "a bee in peace and a wasp in war." She is also called "a mother in Israel" (Judges 5:7). Only four other women in the OT are called prophetesses: Miriam (Ex 15:20), Huldah (2 Ki 22:14), Noadiah (Neh 6:14), and Isaiah's wife (Isa 8:3). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

- **Ellicott** says Deborah is the "only female judge, or, indeed, female ruler of any kind in Jewish history, except the Phoenician murderess, Athaliah." She is the only judge to whom "prophet" is expressly given. "'Prophetess' (like the Latin *Vates*) implies the possession of poetic as well as of prophetic gifts." He compares her to the Teutonic prophetesses Veleda and Alaurinia (Tacitus, *Germania* 8) and Joan of Arc. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html)

- **Gill**: Deborah = "bee," signifying industry, sagacity, sweetness to friends and sharpness to enemies. Lapidoth: most take as her husband's name. Jewish tradition tried to identify Lapidoth with Barak (Barak = "lightning"; Lapidoth = "lamps"), but the context clearly shows otherwise. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/4.htm)

- **Pulpit Homiletics**: The singularity of a woman exercising judicial functions had a powerful effect on the national mind. "A sign this of the decay of the heroic spirit." Yet "she initiates a bold and warlike policy" — rising above the weakness of her sex like Joan of Arc. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/judges/4.htm)

- **Reformed perspective (Ligonier)**: Deborah is a "nationally maternal figure," holding court under a palm tree. "Her positive care for the nation does not inhibit her warrior side." She spurs the men to action like "a mother with a shy son." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/palm-trees-and-tent-pegs)

- **DesiringGod (Baptist/Reformed-leaning)**: The story is not mainly about Deborah. "The primary and sovereign actor in this story is God." Deborah speaks God's word, obeys it, and sings it. She clearly respects Barak's God-ordained role, not belittling or replacing him. She aimed "to lift up Israel's leaders — to encourage them and help them act like leaders." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong)

---

### Verse 5: *"And she would sit under the Palm of Deborah... where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment."*

- **Peaceful arbitration.** Ellicott notes that up to this time her functions "had mainly consisted of peaceful arbitration and legal decision (Deuteronomy 17:8)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html)

- **Location**: between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim — centrally located for Israelites to access her. The palm tree bore her name, suggesting it was a recognized landmark.

- **Enduring Word** addresses the common assumption that Deborah led "because unspecified men failed to take the position." Wolf notes, "Her prominence implies a lack of qualified and willing men." Yet this is an implication, not stated in the text. Deborah was "uniquely called and wonderfully used." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verse 6: *"She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali..."*

- **Deborah never believed God called her alone.** Enduring Word emphasizes she realized God would do much of the work through Barak. The phrase "Has not the LORD God of Israel commanded" suggests Deborah was *confirming* something God had already spoken to Barak. "God often brings confirmation when He speaks to us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Mount Tabor** — a prominent hill in the Jezreel Valley. Barak was to take 10,000 men from Naphtali and Zebulun (northern tribes most directly affected by Jabin's oppression).

---

### Verse 7: *"And I will draw out Sisera... to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand."*

- **Divine strategy.** God promises to lure Sisera's chariots and troops to the Kishon River. The Kishon is a seasonal river that, as Judges 5:21 reveals, became a flooding torrent — disabling the iron chariots in mud. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- Precept Austin cross-references Psalm 83:9, where Sisera's defeat at the Kishon is memorialized along with the Midianites. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_4_commentary)

---

### Verse 8: *"Barak said to her, 'If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.'"*

- **Trusting Deborah's relationship with God more than his own.** Enduring Word says it did not seem unwise for Barak to ask Deborah to come, but the fact that he *demanded* it reveals misplaced trust. F.B. Meyer: "Barak preferred the inspiration of Deborah's presence to the invisible but certain help of Almighty God... He is mentioned in Hebrews 11 as one of the heroes of faith; but his faith lay rather in Deborah's influence with God than in his own." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Trapp** (via Enduring Word): "He is famous for his faith (Hebrews 11:32–33), and yet here he showeth some unbelief. Let us be faithful in weakness, though but weak in faith." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **GotQuestions** simply says Barak was "likely fearful to comply with such a command." (https://www.gotquestions.org/Deborah-and-Barak.html)

- **Constable's Expository Notes**: "Whatever his motivation may have been, he put a condition on obeying God. The will of God was clear. He even had God's promise of victory. Nevertheless he refused to obey unless Deborah accompanied him." Barak's punishment was losing the personal glory of killing Sisera. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-4.html)

---

### Verse 9: *"'I will certainly go with you,' Deborah replied, 'but the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.'"*

- **A prophecy fulfilled unexpectedly.** The reader naturally expects Deborah to be the woman, but the text springs the surprise that it will be Jael — an obscure Kenite wife. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Ellicott**: "This was a prediction which Barak could not understand at the time; but the strain of it conveyed a rebuke of his unmanly fears." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html)

- **Deborah's willingness to go** shows she did not belittle Barak but helped him despite his weakness. She gave God's judgment on his reluctance but still accompanied him. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong)

---

### Verse 10: *"…Ten thousand men followed him, and Deborah also went with him."*

- **"At his feet"** (literal Hebrew) = simply "following him" or "after him" (as in Judges 4:14). Gill notes this emphasizes they were all footmen — Israel had no cavalry, making the victory over chariots all the more miraculous. Josephus reports Sisera had 10,000 horses. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html) and (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/4.htm)

- **Ellicott** adds that the verb translated "called" is the technical term for summoning an army (2 Sam 20:4–5). Zebulun and Naphtali would have been harder to rouse because they'd bear the brunt of vengeance in case of defeat. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-4.html)

---

### Verse 11: *"Now Heber the Kenite had moved away from the Kenites... and had pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim, which was near Kedesh."*

- **Seemingly incidental, but crucial.** Enduring Word explains the Kenites were distant descendants of Israel through Jethro (Moses' father-in-law) back to Abraham through his second wife Keturah (Genesis 25:1–4). Heber had separated from the main body of Kenites. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Ligonier** (Reformed) notes Heber's compromise: "He was at peace with Jabin... Heber was not joining with the other people of Israel against the foe who was persecuting them." This sets up the contrast with Jael, who "knew which side she should be on." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glory-of-jael)

- **Bible.org** (evangelical) argues the hero is not Deborah but Jael, and that Jael took action contradicting her husband's covenant with Jabin — a covenant that was "contrary to God's Word (Exodus 23:32)." She "sought the best interest of her husband, all the while giving obedience to God and His Word highest priority." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/5-strong-women-weak-kneed-wimpy-men-judges-41-24)

---

### Verse 12–13: *"When Sisera was told that Barak... had gone up Mount Tabor, he summoned all nine hundred of his iron chariots..."*

- **A massive show of force.** Enduring Word emphasizes the technological mismatch — 900 iron chariots against foot-soldiers. Sisera mustered everything from Harosheth-hagoyim to the Kishon River. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **The terrain.** Fighting on the plain gave every advantage to chariots. Barak's descent from Mount Tabor into the valley was an act of faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verse 14: *"Then Deborah said to Barak, 'Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?'"*

- **Deborah as encourager and faith-builder.** Enduring Word says "Has not the LORD gone out before you?" is "a phrase that speaks of a king or general leading his troops (1 Samuel 8:20)." Deborah's role was to build up the faith of Barak and his men, reminding them that God Himself would go before them as a warrior-king. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Observe how throughout Deborah takes the lead as the inspired prophetess." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-4.html)

- **Ligonier**: "She does not hesitate at the battle, but spurs the men on to action: 'Up!... Does not the Lord go out before you?'" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/palm-trees-and-tent-pegs)

---

### Verse 15: *"And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot."*

- **The LORD routed them.** Enduring Word notes that Judges 5:4–5 and 5:21 reveal God sent a flash flood. The muddy conditions turned the iron chariots from an advantage into a hindrance. Trapp suggests the "routing" may have involved "thunder and hailstones, as Joshua 10:10; 1 Samuel 7:10" or "some hurry-noise made in the air by the angels, as 2 Kings 6." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **GotQuestions**: "God used a flood to disable the iron chariots of Sisera. The victory was supernatural (verse 20)." (https://www.gotquestions.org/Deborah-and-Barak.html)

- **Barak's faith rewarded.** Poole (via Enduring Word): "He doth not make use of the advantage of the hill, where he might have been out of the reach of his iron chariots... but boldly marcheth down into the valley, to give Sisera the opportunity of using all his horses and chariots, that so the victory might be more glorious and wonderful." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verse 16: *"Then Barak pursued the chariots and army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword; not a single man was left."*

- **Total destruction.** The pursuit covered the distance from the Kishon back to Sisera's base at Harosheth-hagoyim. "Not a single man was left" underscores the completeness of the victory. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verse 17: *"Meanwhile, Sisera had fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite."*

- **The unexpected turn.** Enduring Word notes the reader would assume Deborah would fulfill the prophecy of v. 9, but "God had something else in mind." The LORD used an obscure Kenite wife. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Why Jael's tent?** Poole (via Enduring Word): "Women had their tents apart from their husbands, Genesis 24:67; 31:33. And here he thought to lurk more securely than in her husband's tent." Cundall adds: "Any pursuer would hardly think to look in a woman's tent for any man, let alone a weary fugitive, for this would be a breach of etiquette." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **The peace treaty** between Jabin's kingdom and Heber's household meant Sisera had every reason to trust Jael. (https://www.gotquestions.org/Deborah-and-Barak.html)

---

### Verse 18: *"Jael went out to greet Sisera and said to him, 'Come in, my lord. Come in with me. Do not be afraid.' So he entered her tent, and she covered him with a blanket."*

- **Promise of security.** Poole (via Enduring Word): "This was a promise of security, and therefore she cannot be excused from dissimulation and treachery in the manner, though the substance of her act was lawful and worthy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Ligonier** (Reformed) highlights the blending of instincts: Jael's "nurturing, fighting spirit is clear. She gives him a warm drink, tucks him into bed, and hammers his head to the ground. Neither of these women had to switch off the nurturer inside to let out the warrior." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/palm-trees-and-tent-pegs)

---

### Verse 19: *"Sisera said to her, 'Please give me a little water to drink...' So she opened a container of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again."*

- **Milk, not water.** Giving milk rather than the requested water serves a double purpose in the narrative — warm milk would deepen his drowsiness, aiding her plan. All commentators note this detail.

---

### Verse 20: *"'Stand at the entrance to the tent,' he said, 'and if anyone comes and asks you, "Is there a man here?" say, "No."'"*

- **Sisera's own instructions** sealed his fate. A man entering a woman's tent was a breach of etiquette, so the tent seemed the perfect hiding place. He felt safe enough to relax completely. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verse 21: *"But as he lay sleeping from exhaustion, Heber's wife Jael took a tent peg, grabbed a hammer, and went silently to Sisera. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, and he died."*

- **Ordinary skills, extraordinary use.** Ligonier emphasizes: "Jael was skilled with the tent peg because the women in her day set up and took down the tents. Driving tent pegs accurately and forcefully was second nature for her. And God worked through her to defeat the enemies of His people... God can use ordinary, common skills to accomplish incredible victories." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glory-of-jael)

- **Gory detail = eyewitness account.** Enduring Word: "The gory detail of this matter supports the idea that this was an eye-witness account." Trapp: "Lo, there lay this proud worms' meat sprawling, with his head fastened to the ground, as if it had been now listening to what was become of the soul." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **A breach of hospitality.** Enduring Word acknowledges Jael "broke a fundamental principle of hospitality and many in the ancient world would think her a treacherous woman." Yet God used even her treachery for His purpose: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise You (Psalm 76:10)." Judas's betrayal of Jesus similarly served God's eternal purpose, though Judas still answered for it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "It is impossible for us to view Jael's act in the same light as her contemporaries did, on account of its treachery and cruelty; but we can admire her faith in the God of Israel, her love for the people of God, and her marvellous courage and strength of mind... and make allowance for the age in which she lived." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-4.html)

- **Clarke** (via Enduring Word): "We do not find one word from Jael herself, stating how she was led to do an act repugnant to her feelings as a woman, contrary to good faith, and a breach of the rules of hospitality. Nor does the sacred penman say one word to explain the case... he states the fact, and leaves his readers to form their own opinion." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Poole** (via Enduring Word) suggests Jael was motivated "partly, by observing that the heavens and all the elements conspired against him... partly by the fair opportunity which God's providence put into her hands; and principally, by the secret instinct of God inciting her to it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Spurgeon's typological reading (Baptist)** — Spurgeon preached a sermon titled *Sin Slain*, treating Sisera as a type of sin and Jabin as a type of Satan. His lesson: we should not be content merely to *defeat* sin (as Barak defeated Sisera in battle) but must *kill* it (as Jael did). "If you are content merely to conquer your sins and not to kill them, you may depend upon it, it is the mere work of morality — a surface work — and not the work of the Holy Spirit." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Ligonier on the ethics**: "Jael's actions might seem troublesome given that she used deceit... But this was a time of war, and the rules for war are somewhat different from the rules for peace, with spying and other forms of deceit acceptable in ways that they are not during times of peace (see Josh. 2, for instance)." Moreover, Sisera was "no innocent man" — his people had made normal commerce impossible (Judg 5:6) and were guilty of raping Israelite women (Judg 5:30). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glory-of-jael)

---

### Verse 22: *"When Barak arrived in pursuit of Sisera, Jael went out to greet him and said to him, 'Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.'"*

- **The prophecy fulfilled.** Barak saw Sisera dead, with the tent peg through his temple. The honor of killing Sisera went not to Barak and not to Deborah, but to Jael — exactly as Deborah had prophesied in v. 9. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

---

### Verses 23–24: *"On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. And the hand of the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him."*

- **The war wasn't over with one battle.** Enduring Word: "The battle against Sisera was important, but it did not end the struggle. It was an important event that Israel had to continue to develop and walk in... The war was not over until Jabin was destroyed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **GotQuestions** adds the conclusion from Judges 5:31: "And the land had peace forty years." (https://www.gotquestions.org/Deborah-and-Barak.html)

---

## Traditions Compared

### Where Protestant traditions largely agree

Across the sources consulted, there is broad agreement on the main points: (1) the chapter depicts the fourth Judges cycle; (2) Deborah was uniquely called as both prophetess and judge; (3) Barak's faith was real (Hebrews 11) but mixed with weakness; (4) Jael is the unexpected fulfiller of Deborah's prophecy; (5) God's sovereignty is the driving force — He sent the flood, He routed the army, He subdued Jabin.

### Distinctive emphases

- **Reformed (Ligonier/Enduring Word)**: Strong emphasis on God's sovereignty, the sanctified union of "nurturing and fighting" instincts in godly women, God using ordinary skills (Jael's tent-peg expertise), and the compromised position of Heber. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/palm-trees-and-tent-pegs) and (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glory-of-jael)

- **Reformed Baptist / DesiringGod**: Insists the story is primarily *about God*, not Deborah. Deborah's greatness lies in speaking, obeying, and singing God's word — and in respecting God-ordained male leadership. This reading emphasizes complementarian theology. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-makes-a-woman-strong)

- **Baptist (Spurgeon)**: Reads the narrative typologically — Sisera as sin, Jabin as Satan, Jael's tent peg as the decisive killing of sin. This allegorical approach is distinctive to Spurgeon's preaching tradition. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word)**: David Guzik's commentary (used widely in charismatic circles) emphasizes the prophetic gift operating in women, confirmation of God's word, and the Spirit's "secret instinct" prompting Jael. No prohibition of women in ministry is inferred from the text. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-4/)

- **Evangelical (Bible.org)**: Argues the *heroine* is Jael, not Deborah. Jael is praised for contradicting her husband's sinful covenant with Jabin. This reading focuses on loyalty to God over loyalty to a compromised husband. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/5-strong-women-weak-kneed-wimpy-men-judges-41-24)

---

## What I Could Not Find (due to search limits)

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings**: Searches for newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no results within the search limit. Traditional Catholic commentary (e.g., Haydock) and Orthodox patristic readings are not represented here.

- **Modern scholarship**: bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org searches were not reached. The NET Bible notes on the Kishon flood and archaeological evidence for Hazor would be valuable but were unavailable.

- **Methodist/Wesleyan** (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu) and **Lutheran** (lcms.org, 1517.org) specific commentaries were not reached within the search/fetch limits.

- **Debated modern teachings** (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace readings of Judges 4) were not found in the source list. None of the accessed sites discussed these in connection with Judges 4.
